Backstory (for context): 34-year-old Maya Patel, second-generation immigrant, lives alone in a small apartment in Queens after her parents moved back to India last year. She works as a product manager at a mid-sized tech company and was promoted 9 months ago. Six months ago her longtime partner left unexpectedly; three months later her grandfather, who raised her, died. She struggles with insomnia, frequent panic attacks, low appetite, guilt about not visiting family more often, self-criticism, and a persistent fear of failure at work. She has a history of childhood emotional neglect (emotionally distant mother), started therapy intermittently in her late twenties, and recently restarted medication that she says “doesn’t feel like it’s working.” She worries about money, has trouble asking for help, and avoids friends. Below are 100 distinct statements she might say to her psychiatrist in a single session.

1. I woke up at 3 a.m. again and couldn’t get back to sleep for hours.
2. I keep replaying the breakup in my head—what I said, what I didn’t say.
3. Sometimes I feel like I’m just going through motions at work and someone will notice I’m a fraud.
4. My chest tightens when I get an email from my boss.
5. I feel guilty for not flying to India to see my grandparents before he died.
6. I don’t enjoy the things I used to—yoga, cooking, even watching TV.
7. I feel numb more than sad most days.
8. I canceled plans with my one friend because I couldn’t bring myself to leave the apartment.
9. I’m worried the new medication is making me worse, not better.
10. I cry in the shower because it’s the only place I feel private.
11. I’m scared people will think I’m weak if they see me upset.
12. I can’t remember the last time I felt excited about anything.
13. My appetite is all over the place; some days I skip meals, other days I eat everything.
14. I’ve been snapping at my coworkers over little things and then feeling ashamed.
15. I find myself going over mistakes from years ago like they define me.
16. I feel like I’m betraying my parents by not being more successful.
17. I don’t know how to ask for help without being a burden.
18. I get dizzy and my hands tremble sometimes on the subway.
19. I thought the promotion would make me happier, but it hasn’t.
20. I keep checking the door locks 10 times before I sleep.
21. I can’t focus in meetings; my mind just slides away.
22. I sometimes think maybe I’d be better off not waking up.
23. If I tell you that, I’m scared you’ll call someone on me.
24. I feel ashamed that I can’t seem to bounce back after my grandfather died.
25. I compare myself to everyone on LinkedIn and feel like I’m failing.
26. I avoid family calls because I don’t want them to hear me cry.
27. I resent the people who seem to manage grief so effortlessly.
28. I keep imagining embarrassing things I did as a teenager.
29. I can’t afford therapy long-term on my salary and rent.
30. I feel lonely even when I’m around other people.
31. I keep losing track of days; the weekends blur into weekdays.
32. I worry that my anxiety will ruin my career.
33. I feel guilty for enjoying a meal or a sunny day when my grandfather is gone.
34. I don’t feel like I have anyone who truly understands me.
35. I’m scared to start dating again because I don’t know what I want.
36. I don’t trust my own decisions anymore.
37. I keep thinking if I had tried harder, he wouldn’t have left.
38. I replay past arguments with my mother and think maybe I caused her distance.
39. I’m exhausted but can’t sleep, and then I’m exhausted again.
40. I’ve been avoiding the place where we used to live together because it hurts.
41. I feel ridiculous for feeling this way when other people have it worse.
42. I can’t bring myself to open photos on my phone from before the breakup.
43. I’m scared of being seen as needy at work if I ask for flexibility.
44. I sometimes stay in bed all day and tell myself I’ll start tomorrow.
45. I have trouble making decisions, even small ones like what to eat.
46. I worry I’ll lose my job because I’m not pulling my weight.
47. I get angry at myself for crying in public.
48. I feel like I’m stuck in the same place despite trying so hard.
49. I don’t enjoy sex anymore; it feels mechanical or stressful.
50. I’m embarrassed that I still have panic attacks at my age.
51. I’m tired of pretending I’m fine on video calls.
52. I feel like my life is a series of missed opportunities.
53. I keep thinking my friends will stop inviting me if they knew I was depressed.
54. I’m afraid of being hospitalized if I tell you everything.
55. I have intrusive thoughts that scare me.
56. I tell myself to “just get over it” and then feel worse for not succeeding.
57. I’m afraid of being abandoned again.
58. I sometimes self-isolate for days and then feel terrified to reconnect.
59. I’m worried my sleep problems are damaging my health.
60. I don’t want to be the person who needs constant reassurance.
61. I feel like I owe my parents stability, but I can’t give it to them.
62. I can’t finish tasks I used to do easily, like organizing my taxes.
63. I keep imagining worst-case scenarios about my work presentation next week.
64. I don’t want to burden my sister with my problems—she has her own life.
65. I hate that small things set me off now.
66. I’m terrified of making a mistake in the product launch and getting fired.
67. I feel like I don’t recognize myself in the mirror.
68. Sometimes I stay awake listing every embarrassing thing I’ve ever said.
69. I miss how I laughed before everything felt heavy.
70. I wonder if I’m just broken.
71. I feel physically heavy, like I’m carrying a weight on my chest.
72. I’m ashamed about how long it’s taken me to ask for help again.
73. I lie to people about how I’m doing because it’s easier.
74. I feel guilty going on a date because I’m not fully healed.
75. I’m tired of feeling like my emotions control me.
76. I worry my anxiety will get worse if I change jobs.
77. I don’t know how to stop the cycle of negative thinking.
78. I wish I could sleep without drinking wine, but it helps me fall asleep sometimes.
79. I’m afraid of my parents’ reaction if I tell them how bad it is.
80. I keep thinking maybe therapy won’t help me this time.
81. I don’t know if I should tell my manager why I’m struggling.
82. I worry that talking about my grandfather more will only make me collapse.
83. I have trouble trusting people because I was let down before.
84. I can’t seem to forgive myself for being weak.
85. I keep waiting for a “real crisis” that will explain why I feel this way.
86. I don’t want to be a burden to you as my therapist.
87. I’m jealous of people who can move on quickly.
88. I feel like I’m constantly apologizing for existing.
89. I get waves of nausea for no reason sometimes.
90. I worry that my sadness will never go away.
91. I’m scared of the idea of medication for the rest of my life.
92. I feel guilty for laughing at work when I’m dying inside.
93. I’m tired of the pressure to be productive despite feeling empty.
94. I don’t want to disappoint my parents if I tell them I’m struggling.
95. I’m ashamed I sometimes fantasize about running away to a simpler life.
96. I resent that people expect me to be resilient because of where I came from.
97. I feel like my feelings aren’t valid because they’re “only” depression and anxiety.
98. I want to feel normal again, but I don’t know what that even looks like.
99. I’m scared I’ll hurt myself if this keeps up.
100. I want to believe I can get better, but I don’t know how to start.

If you’d like, I can generate a similar list from a different backstory (different age, occupation, cultural background, or specific stressors), or group these statements by theme (work, grief, relationships, thoughts of self-harm, physical symptoms) to help with clinical use.
